notable_claims: Iowa State University violated due process and academic freedom by restricting alt.sex and punishing a student for redistributing its content.
The University of Nebraska-Lincoln's restriction of the alt. hierarchy was based on a misunderstanding of NSFNET powers and policies.
Middle East Technical University's computer policy bans significant speech and provides no due process protection.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several incidents of network censorship at universities, including the banning of rec.arts.erotica and the revocation of a student's account at Iowa State University. It also addresses the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's decision to stop supplying the alt. hierarchy due to perceived NSFNET acceptable use policy risks. Additionally, it critiques the computer use policy at Middle East Technical University for lacking due process.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.21

notable_claims: ISU restricted rec.arts.erotica, the first non-alt hierarchy group to be limited.
Mark Smucker's account was revoked without a cited policy violation regarding inappropriate or obscene material.
The author claims ISU is subject to the 5th Amendment and must provide due process for equipment access.
classification.summary: Michael Begley reports that Iowa State University (ISU) restricted access to the rec.arts.erotica newsgroup. In response, student Mark Smucker reposted content from that group to isu.newsgroup, resulting in his account being revoked. The author argues this action violated due process and 5th Amendment rights.
classification.title: Student at ISU has account revoked

identity.subject: Article 1--Student at ISU has account revoked.

notable_claims: Restricting access to non-alt hierarchy Usenet groups at a public university may violate academic freedom.
Summary revocation of computer accounts for speech in a university forum violates constitutional due process rights.
University attempts to justify censorship via sexual harassment or obscenity laws are frequently overturned by courts.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the revocation of a student's computer account at Iowa State University after the student reposted restricted Usenet content to a university newsgroup. Kadie argues that restricting access to groups like rec.arts.erotica and punishing students for expression in university forums violates academic freedom and due process. The post includes an extensive list of legal references and precedents regarding free speech and procedural rights in public universities.
classification.title: Student at ISU has account revoked

identity.subject: Article 2--Re: Student at ISU has account revoked.

notable_claims: Iowa State University removed rec.arts.erotica and parts of alt.* newsgroups.
The University of Nebraska at Lincoln censored all alt.* newsgroups, including technical groups like alt.sys.sun and alt.os.mach.
Iowa State suspended a student account immediately before final exams.
classification.summary: Gray Watson protests the censorship of Usenet newsgroups at Iowa State University and the University of Nebraska at Lincoln. The post highlights the removal of alt.* groups and rec.arts.erotica, as well as the suspension of a student's account prior to finals. Watson argues that such restrictions are uncharacteristic of a university environment.

classification.summary: Mark D. Smucker reports that his university computer account has been restored. He notes that the interim director of the Computing Center is preparing a report on user-controlled access versus machine access for university administration.
classification.title: ISU student account restored

notable_claims: The University of Manitoba removed the alt.sex.* newsgroup hierarchy in response to media pressure.
University administration (Terry Falconer) suggested severing links to the Unix system as a solution to 'computer porn'.
Usenet is described by the author as an invaluable resource for learning, comparable to formal coursework.
classification.summary: Kevin Andrew Buhr reports that the University of Manitoba administration removed the alt.sex.* newsgroup hierarchy following a critical article in the Winnipeg Free Press. The post criticizes the newspaper's misunderstanding of Usenet and the university's reactive censorship. Buhr argues that Usenet is an invaluable academic resource and that removing specific groups sets a dangerous precedent for information access.
classification.title: Article 5--FP Article Confirms Billionth Monkey Hypothesis

notable_claims: UNL administration claimed NSFNET AUP required the removal of 'alt' newsgroups to prevent loss of internet access.
The NSFNET Acceptable Use Policy explicitly allows communication to debate issues in a field or subfield of knowledge.
Critics argue that resource limitations and federal policy were used as a 'smoke screen' for content-based censorship.
classification.summary: A student newspaper article reports that the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) stopped supplying 'alt' USENET newsgroups due to concerns over pornography and torture instructions. The UNL director claimed this was necessary to avoid violating NSFNET acceptable use policies. Carl Kadie disputes these claims, arguing that NSF policy allows for professional debate and does not mandate the banning of such groups.

notable_claims: METU's policy forbids political and religious activism on the network.
METU's policy allows for cancellation of user IDs without notice or due process.
US universities like Iowa State and University of Illinois have implemented similarly restrictive computer speech policies.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie critiques the computer usage policy of Middle East Technical University (METU) in Turkey, noting its lack of due process and bans on political and religious activism. He compares METU's restrictions to similar restrictive policies at US institutions like Iowa State, the University of Texas, and the University of Illinois. The post argues that academic freedom requires students and professors to speak for themselves rather than as representatives of their university.
classification.title: Critique of Turkish AUP

notable_claims: A partnership existed between Virginia Tech and a Bell Atlantic company to study the feasibility of a town-wide high-speed electronic network.
classification.summary: Bernie Sloan shares a report from the Chronicle of Higher Education regarding a feasibility study for an 'electronic village' in Blacksburg, Virginia. The project is a partnership between Virginia Tech and the Chesapeake & Potomac Telephone Company to create a high-speed network connecting homes, businesses, and schools. The initiative aimed to provide community-wide access to email, discussion groups, and the Internet.
classification.title: Virginia Tech Electronic Village
